question: Do spatially borrowed, completed forecast innovations improve 30-day earthquake occurrence forecasts beyond adaptive rate and matched calibration?
novelty: Spatial pooling of causally completed forecast errors at multiple memory scales, with cross-region development and a new Alaska geographic audit. Separates forecast-error information from raw neighboring seismic activity.
prior_exposure: Italy and Greece 2020-2026 results were examined in earlier work. New analyses of those cohorts are retrospective development, not fresh confirmation. California and New Zealand previously evaluated in separate work.
development: Italy and Greece origins 2010-2014 train; 2015-2019 validation; 2020-2025 retrospective assessment
external_audit: Alaska newly acquired USGS catalog 2000-2025, Mc=3.0, depth 0-60km, 2-degree cells in [52,72)x[-170,-130). Cells selected with >=30 M>=3 and >=5 M>=3.5 during 2000-2009. New country coefficients selected only using 2010-2019, assessment 2020-2025. No Alaska test scores inspected until architecture and selection are frozen.
features: Original21, direct neighboring rate, spatially shared completed ETAS innovations. Gaussian cell-center spatial weights at 50,100,200 km, self excluded; histories 3,6,12,24 completed 30-day windows; shrunken error normalized by Bernoulli variance; individual-cell innovations retained as ablation.
baselines: Raw and calibrated regional temporal ETAS; adaptive-rate blend; matching logistic/spline/boost complexity; direct-neighbor-rate predictor; annually updated calibration sensitivity. Claims restricted to regional temporal ETAS.
search: All families and hyperparameters specified in code before external evaluation; family selected by validation log loss. No family changes based on Alaska test.
inference: Synchronized time-block bootstrap 3,6,12 origins, 20000 replicates, Holm over 3 audit targets; pooled gain descriptive; cell-year concentration and leave-one-year-out stability.
catalog_caveat: Retrospective preferred catalogs, not real-time versions; completeness and magnitude heterogeneity audited; no physical precursor or universal transfer claim.
